---
title: "Riverine flood-control ecosystem service"
format: html
---

## Purpose

Vegetated landscapes intercept rainfall, slow its passage into rivers and store part of it in
the soil. Where they do so upstream of towns and farmland, floods downstream are shallower than
they would otherwise be, and the damage those floods cause is smaller. That reduction in damage
is what this account values.

The scope is river flooding only. Coastal flooding, storm surge and pluvial flooding lie outside
it, following the hazard product the account uses. The author's pipeline computes on a 537 m
accounting grid. The published table is national: all 250 account rows in USD 2019, of which
162 carry an estimate and 88 carry none.

## Method

Valuing this service requires answering a question that cannot be observed: how much flood damage
would occur if the landscape's vegetation no longer held water back. The account simulates a
counterfactual world with degraded retention, routes the same storms through it, and takes the
difference.

Everything turns on one number per location, the **depth amplification**: the ratio of flood depth
in the degraded world to flood depth in the current one.

### Step 1, how absorbent each piece of land is

A curve number between 30 and 100 is assigned to every cell by crossing land cover with soil
hydrologic group, from USDA field measurements:

$$S = 25400 / \text{CN} - 254$$

$S$ is the potential maximum retention in millimetres. Forest on loam holds 208 mm; the same soil
stripped bare holds 41 mm. This is the only point in the account where vegetation enters the
physics.

### Step 2, how much extra water runs off

$$I_a = 0.2S, \qquad Q = (P - I_a)^2 / (P - I_a + S) \text{ for } P > I_a$$

The relation saturates. As $P$ grows large relative to $S$, runoff approaches total rainfall
regardless of land cover, so the service is concentrated in frequent events and the largest
proportional effects appear where storms are small relative to what the soil can hold.

### Step 3, following the water downhill

$$\text{ratio}(i) = \text{accum}(Q_\text{degraded})(i) / \text{accum}(Q_\text{current})(i)$$

Routing uses MERIT Hydro. On the Upper Mississippi, seven per cent more runoff at the point of
rainfall becomes twenty-two per cent more discharge in the river: routing roughly triples the
local effect, and that is what makes flood regulation a landscape service rather than a local one.

### Step 4, turning more water into deeper water

$$A(i) = [\text{ratio}(i)]^{f}, \qquad f \approx 0.4$$

At-a-station hydraulic geometry gives the split between width, depth and velocity. So 21.5% more
discharge produces 8% more depth. The exponent is the least constrained element of the chain and
is swept over 0.3 to 0.5.

### The depth-damage table

Damage per square metre at each depth comes from the JRC global depth-damage functions (Huizinga
et al., 2017) as the authors rebuild them (`global_flood_gep` at `c0e49dd`,
`counterfactual/rebuild_damage_table.py`, at its defaults, which the authors' method note records
in section 11.6). The source is `country_landtype_depth_damage.xlsx`: 1,231 rows, 214 countries,
six land types, checked against its recorded sha256 before it is read. Urban land (ESA class 190,
SDA class `artif`) takes the Residential curve on the land-use basis, cropland takes the
Agriculture curve, which the source gives per hectare and the rebuild divides by 10,000, and
pasture takes cropland's. No roads class is priced. A land type a country lacks gives a zero
curve. The cropland and pasture curves are zero for 18 countries: 17 have no Agriculture row and
the Faroe Islands' row is zero. The Residential curves are zero for 18 small countries and
territories, the same 18. Every
value is converted from EUR2010 to USD2019 by one factor, 1.3260896 × 1.16006069 = 1.53834442.

The canonical components table (`country_landtype_flood_damage_JRC_EUR_m2.csv`) is not used: its
Residential curves are zero for every country, so urban land would take no damage. The run
therefore sets `flood_skip_damage_tables`, and `task_rebuild_damage_table` writes the table
Section D reads. The rebuilt table reproduces the authors' two checks in their section 11.7:
196 of 214 urban curves are non-zero at 6 m, and Belgium's is USD2019 246.67 per m² (EUR2010
160.35).

## Two counterfactuals

**Bare soil** removes land cover entirely, setting curve numbers to the fallow values of the
reference tables. This is the world a gross product asks about, and it is the reference the
erosion account uses, so the two services are measured against one hypothetical landscape. That
makes their figures comparable on a common baseline; whether they can be added is an overlap
question the shared baseline does not settle by itself.

**In-situ degradation** raises curve numbers less: soils compacted and canopy thinned, the land
still present. Closer to what realistic degradation would produce, and reported alongside rather
than as a sensitivity.

Bare soil exceeds in-situ by about 2.5, and that ratio is stable to within four per cent across
both hazard products and both treatments of permanent water.

## Lambda

Lambda is 1 for this service. The counterfactual already isolates the ecosystem contribution: it
is a difference between two worlds identical in every respect except the ecosystem, so whatever
remains in the difference is the ecosystem's doing by construction.

The **prevention share** reported throughout is a different quantity and not an attribution
coefficient:

$$\text{prevention share} = (\text{EAD}_\text{degraded} - \text{EAD}_\text{current}) / \text{EAD}_\text{degraded}$$

An attribution share near 1 and a prevention share near 0.01 are not two estimates of one thing.

## Sign conventions

GEP is positive: it is damage that does not occur. Degradation raises expected annual damage, so
the difference is non-negative by construction and a negative value indicates a routing or
alignment fault rather than a result.

## Compute

The amplification field is built from rainfall and flow direction rather than from the hazard
maps, so it survives a change of hazard product. Building it is two weeks of single-threaded flow
accumulation over 75 billion cells; everything downstream of it is hours. The author's `RUN.md`
documents both paths.


## Before trusting any rerun of the pipeline

`gep_calculation` publishes the computed bare-counterfactual table when the chain has produced
one — a computed table without the bare column is refused rather than silently substituted — and
the author's per-country export otherwise, recording which was used. The saved published table
was written from the author's export and equals it on all 250 rows (162 with an estimate, 88
missing, identical missingness, largest numeric difference 0). That is a check of the import,
not a reproduction of the pipeline. This section is the warning label for anyone rerunning the
upstream pipeline.

### The failure that made this account wrong twice

The author's `RUN.md` is explicit, and it is the most important thing in it:

> Check flow-direction coverage. This is not optional, and it is the reason this account was wrong
> twice.

Seven MERIT flow-direction packages were missing at various points, and **every absence was
silent**. Accumulation over a missing network writes nodata, the amplification clips to a minimum of
1.0, and the valuation reads 1.0 as *no change here* rather than *no data here*. Japan, Korea,
Portugal and Kazakhstan returned zero service against **49 bn USD of exposure**; Nigeria, Chad,
Cameroon, Niger and the Central African Republic another **4 bn**. Nothing in any log recorded a
problem. Both were found because a country looked implausible. Recovering them raised GEP by
**18.5 per cent and then a further 16**.

    python prep_merit_dir.py --check-tiles

⚠ **The check has a limit the author states plainly.** Its reference list was generated from a tile
set believed complete, so it detects regressions — a lost file, a partial copy, an interrupted
extraction — **but not a package that was never downloaded**, which was the original failure.

A missing amplification raster is refused: `_open_amplification_raster` raises rather than
falling back to current depths, because that fallback completed the job with a wrong zero.
Inside a raster that does open, a nodata cell still reads as an amplification of 1.0
(`_amp_tile`), so the tile check above remains the only guard against a missing flow-direction
package. The author's `RUN.md` carries a three-line check that the mosaic resolves, and his
`msi/final_run.sbatch` verifies the totals itself and prints ALL MATCH or the quantity that
differs.

### Archived run evidence, 2026-09-01 cold start

What follows records that archived run; the current publisher rule is above. Four of the six tasks ran: `task_compute_service_flow`, `task_compute_flood_damages`,
`task_compute_flood_gep` and `task_generate_maps_and_figures`. The GEP chain with the
counterfactuals gave **$11,403,596,548** across 250 rows, positive in 163: that run valued
Iceland at $0.021 where the author's table carries NA, so its NA mask differed by one country,
and the agreement to the cent held on the 162 rows both sides value — shared nonmissing
agreement, not a 250-of-250 match. The CURRENT published table instead is the author's export,
equal on all 250 rows (162 positive, 88 missing, identical missingness, largest numeric
difference 0). In that archived run, `gep = ead_bare - ead_current`
holds to 1.2e-07 on every row, and the damage side reproduces at $887,827,659,820 /
$194,256,309,530 / $551,051,565,602.

The two tasks that do not run here are `task_prepare_flood_inputs` and `task_build_sda`, which are
Sections A and B. That is deliberate on the author's part rather than a gap: his RUN.md tells a
reader to copy the staged Sections B and C across because rebuilding them turns a three-hour run
into an eleven-hour one. A cold start of those two began on 2026-09-01, once the inputs they need
were staged into base_data -- the aligned JRC depths at 1.3 GB and the service-providing-area raster
at 144 MB.

⚠ **What reproducing him does and does not establish.** The module is his pipeline with our path
handling and ProjectFlow wiring, so agreement was close to guaranteed. It is a build test: it
catches our refactor breaking his arithmetic, and says nothing about whether the arithmetic is
right.

⚠ **The water variant moves this figure more than anything else in it.** The run writes four, and
`gep_flood_bare` is $6.29bn on 4rp, $7.34bn on v1_2016, $11.40bn on v2_2024_waterremoved -- the
delivered one -- and $24.54bn on v2_2024_waterkept. Keeping permanent water more than doubles the
headline. The author has reported about $11.4bn consistently, in correspondence and in his committed
table, so waterremoved is the account's variant; the gap is pinned by a test so it cannot drift
unnoticed.

### What running the remaining two needs

The inputs live on MSI at `/projects/standard/jajohns/shared/flood_gep`, read-only. What Sections A
and B actually need from it is small -- `flood_depth_aligned_path` and `flood_spa_path`, 1.5 GB with
the optional population grid -- and both are staged in base_data now with the template carrying the
references. The 129 GB of counterfactual amplification rasters in that tree feed
`task_compute_flood_gep`, which already runs, so they are not part of this.
